title: My own fruit
hookLine: the rational soul sees itself, shapes itself, and gathers its own fruit (Meditations 11.1)

cards: An apple tree grows an apple, and someone else eats it. A cow makes milk, and someone else drinks it. A vine grows grapes for somebody's table.

Plants and animals, Marcus says, bear fruit that others enjoy. Book eleven of the Meditations opens with him noticing one kind of fruit that's different, one harvest that stays with the one who grows it.

teach.b: First, the mirror. The reasoning soul, Marcus says, sees itself, examines itself, and shapes itself into whatever it chooses. No plant can look at itself and decide to grow differently.

The fruit it bears, he says, it gathers for itself. A tree's fruit and an animal's yield are enjoyed by others. But the fruit of a well-lived life, steadiness, kindness, clear sight, belongs to the one who grew it.
You don't have to wait for someone else to taste it. Third, whole at every point. A dance or a play, Marcus says, is left incomplete if it's cut off partway.
But the soul reaches its own end wherever life stops. Each act done well is whole in itself, so at any moment it can say: I have what is my own.
The soul ranges over the whole universe and the emptiness around it, stretches into endless time, and sees that those who come after us will see nothing new.
A person of forty, he adds, with any understanding at all, has in a sense seen everything that has been and will be: the same patterns keep coming round.
And closer to home, look honestly at yourself, and the harvest is already yours.

how: Some readers of the Meditations end the day with a short, honest look at themselves, naming one good thing they grew and one thing to shape differently tomorrow.

games.why: a dance or play is incomplete if interrupted, he writes, but the soul completes its work wherever it stops, and can say: I have what is my own.

practice: Look at yourself for a minute the way you'd look at a friend you love, not judging, just seeing, and name one fruit you grew this week: patience in one place, a kept promise, a kind word at the right time.
Gather it yourself, without waiting for anyone else to notice. Then notice one thing you'd like to shape differently, and simply set the intention.

wordCard.voice: Marcus, who said the reasoning soul sees itself, shapes itself, and gathers its own harvest, whole at every point. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: fruit, harvest. Marcus says the soul gathers its own karpos.

carryVoice: Your line: gather your own harvest. Nobody else has to taste it for it to be real. Until tomorrow.
